subject: physics

items.q: The specification defines momentum by an equation. Which word equation is that definition?
items.correct: momentum = mass × velocity
items.misconception: momentum = mass × acceleration
items.why: F = m a and p = m v are met close together, both begin with mass, and 'momentum' sounds like the everyday idea of building up speed — which is acceleration. Separate the two: mass × velocity is momentum, in kg m/s; mass × acceleration is resultant force, in newtons. An object at constant velocity has momentum but no acceleration.
items.random_wrong: momentum = weight × velocity

items.q: The momentum equation is written in symbols as p = m v. What do p, m and v stand for?
items.correct: momentum, mass and velocity
items.misconception: power, mass and velocity
items.why: The letter p is genuinely used for both power and pressure elsewhere in the course, and momentum has no obvious link to the letter p, so the older meanings win. Learn this symbol list as a set: momentum, p, in kg m/s; mass, m, in kg; velocity, v, in m/s. The unit is the giveaway — kg m/s can only be momentum.
items.random_wrong: pressure, mass and velocity

items.q: Which of these is the unit of momentum given in the specification?
items.correct: the kilograms metre per second, kg m/s
items.misconception: the newton, N, the same unit as force
items.why: Momentum is introduced alongside force, and the everyday sense of momentum is 'how hard something hits'. The newton is the unit students associate with impact. Build the unit from the equation: kilograms multiplied by metres per second gives kg m/s. Newtons belong to force, which is the rate of change of momentum, not momentum itself.
items.random_wrong: the joule, J, the same unit as energy

items.q: A ball of mass 250 g is travelling at 6 m/s. What is its momentum?
items.correct: 1.5 kg m/s
items.misconception: 1500 kg m/s
items.why: The equation is remembered as an arithmetic instruction, and the numbers given in a question feel authorised for use. Nothing in the calculation itself fails to warn the student. The specification states mass, m, in kilograms, kg. Convert grams to kilograms by dividing by 1000 before substituting anything.
items.random_wrong: 0.75 kg m/s

items.q: Which statement about the units used in p = m v is correct?
items.correct: The velocity must be in m/s and the mass in kg.
items.misconception: The velocity must be in m/s and the mass in g.
items.why: The equation is remembered as an arithmetic instruction, and the numbers given in a question feel authorised for use. Nothing in the calculation itself fails to warn the student. The specification states mass, m, in kilograms, kg. Convert grams to kilograms by dividing by 1000 before substituting anything.
items.random_wrong: The velocity must be in km/h and the mass in kg.

items.q: A sprinter of mass 60 kg is running at 8 m/s. What is the sprinter's momentum?
items.correct: 480 kg m/s
items.misconception: 240 kg m/s
items.why: Kinetic energy, ½ m v², is met earlier in the same topic and also contains mass and velocity, so the two equations blur together and the ½ or the squaring migrates across. Keep the two apart: kinetic energy is ½ m v² in joules; momentum is m v in kg m/s. Momentum has no ½ and the velocity is not squared.
items.random_wrong: 3840 kg m/s

items.q: A lorry of mass 8000 kg is moving at 2 m/s. A car of mass 1000 kg is moving at 20 m/s. Which has the greater momentum?
items.correct: The car, because 1000 × 20 gives 20 000 kg m/s.
items.misconception: The lorry, because its mass is eight times larger.
items.why: Mass is the first quantity in the equation and the most vivid feature of a lorry, so students compare the masses and stop there instead of completing the multiplication. Neither quantity decides on its own. Work out mass × velocity for both objects before making any comparison.
items.random_wrong: They are equal, as the mass and speed compensate.

items.q: A van of mass 900 kg has a momentum of 3600 kg m/s. What is its velocity?
items.correct: 4 m/s
items.why: Rearrangement is done by pattern-matching rather than algebra, and dividing whichever way produces a tidy number feels like a check that it was done correctly. Rearrange the symbols first, then substitute: v = p / m. Then test the units — kg m/s divided by kg leaves m/s, which is a velocity.
items.random_wrong: 8 m/s

items.q: A student works out the momentum of a trolley and writes the answer as '12 N'. What is wrong with this?
items.correct: The unit should be kg m/s, since momentum is mass × velocity.
items.misconception: Nothing is wrong; momentum is a force, so newtons are right.
items.why: Momentum is introduced alongside force, and the everyday sense of momentum is 'how hard something hits'. The newton is the unit students associate with impact. Build the unit from the equation: kilograms multiplied by metres per second gives kg m/s. Newtons belong to force, which is the rate of change of momentum, not momentum itself.
items.random_wrong: The unit should be joules, since momentum is a form of energy.

items.q: Which of these completes the specification's statement of conservation of momentum correctly?
items.correct: In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total after it.
items.misconception: In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is greater than the total after it.
items.why: Students judge momentum by how fast things are moving and see the drop in speed as a drop in momentum. Energy really is dissipated in such a collision, which reinforces the idea that something has been lost. Check with numbers. Mass before is 2 kg at 3 m/s, giving 6 kg m/s; mass afterwards is 3 kg at 2 m/s, also 6 kg m/s. The total is unchanged in a closed system.
items.random_wrong: In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is shared equally after it.

items.q: What name does the specification give to the rule that the total momentum of a closed system is the same before and after an event?
items.correct: the conservation of momentum
items.misconception: Newton's Second Law of motion
items.why: F = m a and p = m v are met close together, both begin with mass, and 'momentum' sounds like the everyday idea of building up speed — which is acceleration. Separate the two: mass × velocity is momentum, in kg m/s; mass × acceleration is resultant force, in newtons. An object at constant velocity has momentum but no acceleration.
items.random_wrong: the principle of moments

items.q: Trolley A has a mass of 2 kg and moves at 3 m/s towards a stationary 1 kg trolley B. The two trolleys form a closed system. What is their total momentum immediately after the collision?
items.correct: 6 kg m/s
items.misconception: 3 kg m/s
items.why: The forces on the two skaters really are equal in size, and students slide from equal forces to equal speeds without going through mass. Equal and opposite momenta, not equal speeds. Set 60 × 1.5 equal to 45 × v and solve: v = 2 m/s, faster than the heavier skater.
items.random_wrong: 9 kg m/s

items.q: A moving snooker ball strikes a stationary ball of equal mass head-on and stops dead. Which description of this event is correct?
items.correct: All the momentum has been transferred to the second ball.
items.misconception: The momentum of the first ball has simply disappeared.
items.why: Students judge momentum by how fast things are moving and see the drop in speed as a drop in momentum. Energy really is dissipated in such a collision, which reinforces the idea that something has been lost. Check with numbers. Mass before is 2 kg at 3 m/s, giving 6 kg m/s; mass afterwards is 3 kg at 2 m/s, also 6 kg m/s. The total is unchanged in a closed system.
items.random_wrong: Both balls now share the momentum equally between them.

items.q: A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley, and the two move off joined together. What is their velocity after the collision?
items.correct: 2 m/s
items.misconception: 3 m/s
items.why: The stationary trolley contributed nothing before the collision, so students carry on ignoring it afterwards, even though it is now part of the moving object. After the objects join there is one object. Its mass is the sum of the two masses, and that is what the total momentum is divided by.
items.random_wrong: 6 m/s

items.q: A 0.5 kg ball moving to the right at 4 m/s meets a 0.3 kg ball moving to the left at 2 m/s. Taking right as the positive direction, what is the total momentum of the two balls before they collide?
items.correct: 1.4 kg m/s to the right
items.misconception: 2.6 kg m/s to the right
items.why: 'Total' is read as 'add everything up'. Direction has been carried through velocity all year, but with a new quantity students revert to treating the numbers as plain sizes. Momentum has direction because velocity does. Choose one direction as positive, make the opposite one negative, and then add.
items.random_wrong: 0.8 kg m/s to the right

items.q: Two skaters stand at rest on ice and push each other apart. One has a mass of 60 kg and moves off at 1.5 m/s. The other has a mass of 45 kg. What is her velocity?
items.correct: 2 m/s
items.why: The forces on the two skaters really are equal in size, and students slide from equal forces to equal speeds without going through mass. Equal and opposite momenta, not equal speeds. Set 60 × 1.5 equal to 45 × v and solve: v = 2 m/s, faster than the heavier skater.

items.q: The specification states what happens when a force acts on an object that is moving, or able to move. What occurs?
items.correct: a change in the momentum of the object
items.misconception: a change in the weight of the object
items.why: 'Weight' and 'mass' are interchangeable in everyday speech, and both are stated as single numbers describing how heavy something is. Check the unit before substituting. Mass, m, is in kilograms, kg; a value in newtons is a force and must be converted using weight = mass × gravitational field strength.
items.random_wrong: an increase in momentum, never a decrease

items.q: Which two equations does the specification combine to give F = (m ∆v)/(∆t)?
items.correct: F = m × a and a = (v − u)/t
items.misconception: E = ½ m v² and a = (v − u)/t
items.why: Kinetic energy, ½ m v², is met earlier in the same topic and also contains mass and velocity, so the two equations blur together and the ½ or the squaring migrates across. Keep the two apart: kinetic energy is ½ m v² in joules; momentum is m v in kg m/s. Momentum has no ½ and the velocity is not squared.
items.random_wrong: W = F s and a = (v − u)/t

items.q: A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 20 m/s is brought to rest in 0.10 s when it hits a wall. Using F = (m ∆v)/(∆t), which is given on the equation sheet, what is the average force on the car?
items.why: 'Force equals the rate of change of momentum' is compressed in memory to 'force equals change of momentum', and m ∆v is the part of the equation that gets calculated first. The equation is F = (m ∆v)/(∆t). The division by time is what turns a change in momentum into a force, and it is what makes the units newtons rather than kg m/s.

items.q: In the equation F = (m ∆v)/(∆t), what does the quantity m ∆v represent?
items.correct: the change in momentum of the object
items.misconception: the mass times the final velocity
items.why: The delta symbol is new and easily read as decoration on the letter v rather than as an instruction to subtract. Many earlier equations do use the final velocity directly. ∆ always means 'change in'. Write down the initial and final velocities and subtract before substituting anything.
items.random_wrong: the total momentum of the object

items.q: The specification says that force equals the rate of change of momentum. What does 'rate of change of momentum' mean?
items.correct: the change in momentum divided by the time taken
items.misconception: the total momentum divided by the time taken
items.why: 'Rate of' is correctly read as 'divided by time', but 'change of' is skipped, so the total momentum is used where the change should be. Two steps every time: first find the change in momentum, m ∆v, then divide by ∆t. For an object slowing from 20 m/s to 15 m/s, ∆v is 5 m/s, not 15 m/s.
items.random_wrong: the change in momentum multiplied by the time

items.q: A car is fitted with an air bag, which inflates in front of the driver during a crash. Why does the air bag reduce the force on the driver?
items.correct: It makes the driver's momentum change over a longer time.
items.misconception: It makes the change in the driver's momentum much smaller.
items.why: Students know the safety feature makes the crash gentler and attach that to the only quantity in the equation they can name, without noticing that the driver's speed before the crash and their speed afterwards are both fixed. Ask what the driver's velocity is before and after: unchanged by the bag. Only the time is changed, and F = (m ∆v)/(∆t) then gives a smaller force.
items.random_wrong: It brings the driver to a stop far more quickly and safely.

items.q: A gymnast lands on a thick crash mat rather than on the bare floor. Which explanation of the mat's effect is correct?
items.correct: The mat increases the stopping time, so the force is less.
items.misconception: The mat reduces the gymnast's momentum on landing.
items.why: Students know the safety feature makes the crash gentler and attach that to the only quantity in the equation they can name, without noticing that the driver's speed before the crash and their speed afterwards are both fixed. Ask what the driver's velocity is before and after: unchanged by the bag. Only the time is changed, and F = (m ∆v)/(∆t) then gives a smaller force.
items.random_wrong: The mat stops the gymnast in a much shorter time.

items.q: Two identical cars, each of mass 1200 kg, hit a wall at 20 m/s. Car A stops in 0.10 s. Car B has a crumple zone and stops in 0.50 s. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The force on car B is one fifth of the force on car A.
items.misconception: Car B's change in momentum is five times smaller than car A's.
items.why: Students know the safety feature makes the crash gentler and attach that to the only quantity in the equation they can name, without noticing that the driver's speed before the crash and their speed afterwards are both fixed. Ask what the driver's velocity is before and after: unchanged by the bag. Only the time is changed, and F = (m ∆v)/(∆t) then gives a smaller force.
items.random_wrong: The force on car B is the same, because the cars are identical.

items.q: A lorry of mass 12 000 kg is parked at the side of the road. What is its momentum?
items.correct: zero, since its velocity is zero
items.misconception: 12 000 kg m/s, from its mass alone
items.why: Momentum is talked about as if it were a possession, like mass, rather than something that depends on motion. A parked lorry still feels 'powerful'. Momentum depends on velocity as well as mass. Zero velocity gives zero momentum, no matter how large the mass.
items.random_wrong: very large, because its mass is large

items.q: A bullet travels much faster than a lorry. Does the bullet have the greater momentum?
items.correct: No. Momentum is mass × velocity, and the lorry's enormous mass more than makes up for its low speed.
items.misconception: Whichever object is moving faster must have the more momentum — momentum is basically about speed.
items.why: In everyday language 'momentum' is used to mean something like unstoppable speed, and the examples students meet first (a fast ball, a speeding car) vary the speed while leaving the mass unmentioned. Always calculate. Multiply mass by velocity for each object and compare the two numbers; a large mass at a small velocity often wins.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A rolling ball slows to a stop against a rough carpet. Is momentum conserved?
items.correct: Not for the ball alone. Friction from the carpet is an external force, so the ball on its own is not a closed system.
items.misconception: Momentum is always conserved, in every situation, whatever else is going on.
items.why: The rule is remembered as a slogan — 'momentum is conserved' — with the opening words 'in a closed system' dropped as scene-setting rather than a condition. Quote the statement in full: in a closed system, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total momentum after the event. If an external force acts, the condition is not met.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a crash mat work by stopping the gymnast more quickly?
items.correct: No — the opposite. The mat squashes, so the gymnast takes longer to stop and the force on them is smaller.
items.misconception: Safety features bring you to a stop faster, and stopping fast is what keeps you safe.
items.why: Safety is associated with braking quickly from road-safety teaching about stopping distances, so 'stops you quickly' sounds like a virtue in any context. Stopping quickly means a large rate of change of momentum, which means a large force. Every one of the safety features named works by stretching the stopping time out.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a cycle helmet absorb the force of an impact?
items.correct: The helmet's foam crushes, so the head is brought to rest over a longer time and the force on the head is reduced.
items.misconception: The helmet soaks up the force and holds it, so less of it reaches you.
items.why: Force is imagined as a substance that flows and can be stored, like water in a sponge. The word 'absorb' is used loosely in adverts and in everyday talk about padding. Force is an interaction, not a substance, and cannot be stored. Explain in terms of time: the crushing foam extends ∆t, so F = (m ∆v)/(∆t) is smaller.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A car doubles its velocity. What happens to its momentum?
items.correct: It doubles. Momentum is proportional to velocity, since p = m v.
items.misconception: It becomes four times as big, because doubling the velocity has a squared effect.
items.why: Kinetic energy really does quadruple when velocity doubles, and that striking fact is taught in the same unit. Students carry the squared relationship over to momentum. Look at the equation. Velocity appears to the power one in p = m v, so momentum simply doubles; it is ½ m v² that quadruples.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In p = m v, is v the volume of the object?
items.correct: No, v is velocity, in metres per second.
items.misconception: v means volume, so momentum is worked out from mass and volume, like density.
items.why: Density, ρ = m/V, is met in the same course and uses m and V together, so a formula containing m and v looks like a version of it. Check the units the specification gives: velocity, v, in metres per second, m/s. Volume would give a unit of kg m³, which is not the unit of momentum.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A braking force acts on a moving van. Is its momentum changing?
items.correct: Yes. A change in momentum occurs whenever a force acts on an object that is moving, or able to move — here the momentum is decreasing.
items.misconception: A force can only give an object more momentum; slowing down is momentum being lost rather than changed.
items.why: Forces are introduced as things that get objects going, and 'change' is heard as 'increase'. A decrease looks like the absence of a change rather than a change with the opposite sign. A change in momentum can be an increase or a decrease. The direction of the force decides which: a force opposing the motion reduces the momentum.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
